claims.text: Rapidly quenched Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 can largely retain an amorphous state.
Low-concentration carbon doping will improve the glass-forming ability of phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys.
Low-concentration carbon doping will improve the thermal stability of the amorphous phase in phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys.
The intervention requires cooling sufficiently rapid to bypass crystallization.
The beneficial effect of carbon will diminish under slower cooling conditions that favor crystallization.
Excessive carbon may produce unwanted carbide phases.
Carbon-metal interactions increase atomic-packing disorder and heterogeneity.
Atomic-size and bonding heterogeneity disrupt crystal nucleation and long-range crystalline ordering.
Carbon's small atomic size and strong covalent or mixed bonding increase local configurational entropy.
Increasing configurational entropy lowers the Gibbs free energy of the amorphous phase and favors it over crystalline phases.
The carbon-induced reduction in amorphous-phase Gibbs free energy resists crystallization during and after rapid solidification.
Carbon-doped samples will have a greater amorphous fraction than undoped samples processed identically.
Carbon doping will produce a higher critical cooling rate for amorphization.
Carbon-doped samples will have a higher DSC crystallization-onset temperature than undoped samples.
The optimal carbon concentration and the magnitude of its benefit depend on processing conditions and alloy composition.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis claims improved glass-forming ability, but the predicted outcome specifies a higher critical cooling rate. Within the usual definition of glass-forming ability, improvement corresponds to achieving amorphization at a lower, not higher, critical cooling rate.
